title: Scheduler policy simulations notes (SRPT vs two-queue) — mixed-workload prototype
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We needed a quick, rough way to sanity-check whether “short/long aware” scheduling should improve p95 for short prompts under mixed traffic, and what knobs matter (threshold, share, aging).
- This is NOT a faithful model of the runtime. It’s a queueing-style simulation with some attempt to map “prefill vs decode” cost, plus a crude batching effect.
- Primary question: under the same offered load, does class-based scheduling move the p95 needle for short requests without catastrophic long-tail regressions?

High-level summary (current conclusion)
- Two-queue with a fixed short-priority share + aging looks like the best “simple + robust” policy in simulation.
- Pure SRPT (job-size-based priority) is best for mean + p95 in the toy model, but is brittle under misprediction and can be unpleasant for fairness / multi-tenant optics. Also it doesn’t map cleanly to our prefill/decode pipeline unless we do preemption or chunking.
- Main mismatch with production: batching + kernel selection makes service time non-linear; and prefill can monopolize the batch selection step. Our simulation underestimates that head-of-line blocking effect (which is precisely why separating prefill/decode scheduling matters).

Simulation setup
1) Entities
- A “request” i has:
  - prompt_tokens (prefill tokens)
  - decode_tokens (generated tokens; either fixed target or geometric)
  - arrival_time
  - service_time estimate = prefill_cost(prompt_tokens) + decode_cost(decode_tokens)
- We track:
  - TTFT proxy (time until first decode step completes)
  - end-to-end latency proxy
  - time in queue

2) Arrival process
- Baseline: Poisson arrivals with rate λ.
- Mixed workload: short and long are a mixture distribution.
  - short: prompt_tokens ~ Uniform(20, 200), decode_tokens ~ Uniform(16, 256)
  - long: prompt_tokens ~ Uniform(2k, 12k), decode_tokens ~ Uniform(64, 512)
- Mix ratios tested: 80/20, 50/50, and “long spikes” (bursty long arrivals for 30s windows).
- Note: we also ran a “diurnal burst” version where λ(t) is piecewise constant (to mimic production ramps) — results qualitatively similar but with bigger variance.

3) Service model (single GPU abstraction)
- We model one server with capacity 1.0 “GPU units” and discrete scheduling ticks.
- Each tick, scheduler selects a batch from the queue and serves it.
- Crude batching effect:
  - If batch_size = B, effective per-token cost is reduced by factor f(B) up to a cap.
  - f(B) = min(1.0, 0.75 + 0.25/B) for prefill and min(1.0, 0.70 + 0.30/B) for decode (totally heuristic).
- Prefill vs decode separation:
  - In the simplest version, prefill+decode is one job (non-preemptive).
  - In the improved version, we “chunk” decode into decode_quanta (e.g., 16 tokens) so scheduling can interleave decode between requests, which better matches our continuous batching decode loop.
  - Prefill is still non-preemptive in the model unless we enable “prefill chunking” (we tried, but it didn’t map well to the actual kernel path).

4) Classification
- Two classes: short vs long.
- Thresholds tested:
  - by prompt_tokens: 512, 1024, 2048
  - by estimated prefill_cost: equivalent thresholds derived from linear prefill cost model
- In the runs below, “short” is prompt_tokens <= 1024 unless otherwise noted.

5) Policies tested
A) FIFO
- Single queue, pick oldest.

B) SRPT (Shortest Remaining Processing Time)
- Priority by predicted remaining service time.
- Variants:
  - perfect size knowledge
  - noisy size prediction: multiplicative lognormal noise (σ = 0.4) on total service time

C) Two-queue (short/long)
- Maintain Qs, Ql.
- Each scheduling decision:
  - serve from Qs until short_share budget is met (e.g., 70% of ticks), else serve from Ql.
  - aging: long requests gain “priority credits” the longer they wait; after max_wait_ms they can preempt the share rule.
- Knobs:
  - short_share: 60/70/80%
  - aging_half_life_ms: 250/500/1000
  - max_consecutive_short: 8/16/32 ticks

D) Weighted fair token scheduling (toy)
- Similar to two-queue but budgets by estimated tokens rather than ticks.
- More stable in some scenarios, but sensitive to estimate accuracy.

Key outputs / results (toy numbers)
Important: absolute values are not to be trusted. Deltas and qualitative behavior are what we care about.

Scenario 1: 80/20 mix, moderate load (ρ ~ 0.75)
- Threshold: 1024 prompt tokens

Metrics reported: p50/p95 end-to-end for short, p95 for long, and throughput (req/s). Throughput is “completed requests per simulated second” and is mostly constant across policies at fixed load (differences are from idling due to caps).

Policy                    Short p50    Short p95    Long p95     Notes
FIFO                      0.42s        2.9s         9.8s         long prefill blocks short behind it
SRPT (perfect)            0.36s        1.1s         12.4s        best short p95; long tail worsens
SRPT (σ=0.4 noise)        0.38s        1.6s         11.8s        still good but worse; occasional mis-ordering
Two-queue 70% + aging     0.37s        1.4s         10.6s        good win; long tail contained w/ aging
Two-queue 80% + aging     0.36s        1.2s         14.9s        long p95 blows up unless aging is aggressive
Weighted token budgets    0.37s        1.3s         11.3s        close to 70% two-queue, but brittle w/ noise

Takeaway:
- Two-queue at ~70% share gets most of the SRPT win for short p95 without “obviously unfair” long p95 inflation.
- Share higher than ~70–75% needs a strong anti-starvation mechanism (max_wait or credit-based override).

Scenario 2: 50/50 mix, moderate-high load (ρ ~ 0.85)

Policy                    Short p95    Long p95     Observations
FIFO                      6.8s         14.0s        everything is bad; system saturates
SRPT (perfect)            2.9s         22.7s        short gets rescued; long suffers hard
Two-queue 70% + aging     3.4s         17.2s        trade-off feels acceptable; still heavy load
Two-queue 60% + aging     4.1s         15.1s        better for long; short p95 worsens

Takeaway:
- Under heavier mixes, two-queue is mostly about picking where the pain lands.
- We probably want default short_share to be “conservative” (60–70) and make it SKU/pool-tunable.

Scenario 3: Long spike (80/20 baseline, but long arrivals spike to 50% for 30s)
- Main question: does short p95 stay protected, and do we recover once spike ends?

Policy                    Short p95 during spike   Recovery time to baseline p95   Notes
FIFO                      +4–6x                  slow (minutes)                    queue builds; drains slowly
SRPT (perfect)            +1.2–1.5x              fast (tens of seconds)            long queue becomes huge
Two-queue 70% + aging     +1.4–2.0x              moderate (1–2 min)                depends on max_wait/credits
Two-queue 70% no aging    +1.1–1.3x              N/A (long starves)                unacceptable: long queue can diverge

Takeaway:
- Aging is not optional.
- There is a real “recovery” dynamic: protecting short too aggressively defers long work and makes post-spike recovery slower.

Sensitivity notes
- Threshold choice (short vs long):
  - 512 tokens: short class gets “too small” and we end up protecting an extremely small set; not enough improvement for typical chat prompts (which can be >512 easily).
  - 1024 tokens: best compromise in toy model.
  - 2048 tokens: short class includes a chunk of long-context-ish requests; short p95 improves less, and the head-of-line blocking comes back.
- Prediction noise hurts SRPT more than it hurts two-queue.
- If we model decode chunking (quantum 16 tokens), SRPT benefits slightly less (already good), while two-queue benefits more (interleaving makes the share mechanism more effective).

What matched production (qualitative)
- Even a simple short/long split can reduce p95 for “short” under mixed traffic.
- If you don’t include starvation prevention, long requests can get stuck forever under sustained short load.
- Aggressive short priority can create “long debt,” which bites later (recovery time).

What did NOT match production (and likely why)
1) Prefill domination is worse in prod
- In the real runtime, a single long prefill can dominate GPU time and also influence batch composition decisions.
- The toy batching model (f(B)) is too smooth and doesn’t capture the discrete/step-function nature of kernel choices.

2) Kernel selection instability / “thrash”
- Production had cases where mixing sequence lengths triggered different kernels and caused effective service rate to drop.
- In the sim, service rate is mostly fixed (only mild batching benefit), so we miss the second-order effect: scheduling policy can change sequence-length distribution per batch, which changes kernel selection, which changes throughput, which feeds back into queueing.

3) KV cache pressure and eviction
- Real behavior: long contexts pressure KV cache and can increase cache management overhead; also interacts with compaction/fragmentation.
- Sim has no cache. So the “cost” of serving long requests in real life is often higher than token counts suggest, and can be bursty.

4) Admission control / backpressure
- In prod, we have upstream timeouts, rate limits, and sometimes load shedding that truncates the tail (or moves it elsewhere).
- Sim assumes infinite buffers.

5) Multi-GPU / multi-worker realities
- We simulate a single server; real pools have N workers and request routing across them.
- Cross-worker imbalance and sticky routing can dominate tail in some cases.

Notes on policy choice: SRPT vs two-queue
- SRPT is theoretically appealing (great for mean response time), but:
  - needs a good remaining-time estimate (we don’t reliably have it for decode, esp. streaming/stop conditions)
  - can look unfair; hard to explain/justify in multi-tenant contexts
  - true SRPT wants preemption; our pipeline only naturally supports “soft preemption” via decode chunking, not prefill
- Two-queue is “good enough,” tunable, and easier to reason about operationally:
  - we can say: short prompts get X share unless long has been waiting too long
  - knobs map to config + SRE guardrails

Open questions / next steps
- Can we base classification on predicted prefill cost (or attention FLOPs proxy) instead of raw prompt_tokens? Might reduce threshold churn across models.
- How should share be expressed in the real scheduler?
  - by iterations/ticks? by tokens? by prefill vs decode time?
  - token budgets per class (PR-24872 direction) seem closer to reality than “ticks” in the sim.
- What is the right aging function?
  - linear wait-time credits vs exponential/half-life
  - need a bound that’s easy to validate and test
- Add a “kernel penalty” term to the sim?
  - e.g., if a batch spans length buckets, apply a throughput penalty to mimic kernel thrash
  - might help us predict the scary cases we saw in early perf runs

Appendix: knobs we used most in discussion
- short_threshold_prompt_tokens = 1024
- short_share = 0.70 (60–70 looked safe; 80 risky)
- max_wait_ms_long = 1500–2500ms (in sim; needs mapping to prod SLOs)
- decode_quantum_tokens = 16

Loose mapping to implementation work
- The sim supports the direction of:
  - two-queue dispatch (PR-24844)
  - explicit starvation prevention (follow-up PR-24905)
  - per-class token budgets as a guardrail (PR-24872)
- BUT it doesn’t prove any specific default values. Those should be set by benchmark lab + trace replay + canary.
